chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from one of his companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He was asked about the limit of the miles at which shortening (of prayer) becomes obligatory. So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) set the limit of the miles from the shade of 'Ayr to the shade of Wueyr, and these two are mountains in Medina. So when the sun rises, the shadow of 'Ayr falls to the shadow of Wueyr, and that is the mile upon which the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) placed the ruling of shortening.'

key_terms.التَّقْصِيرُ: Shortening of the four-rakat prayer to two rakats for travelers

ai.seo_question: What is the specific distance in miles at which a Muslim traveler must shorten their prayers according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi grounds the legal concept of *qasr* (shortening prayer) in a tangible, historical geographical marker from Medina—the distance between the shadows of Mounts 'Ayr and Wueyr at sunrise—demonstrating the Prophet's practical approach to defining travel boundaries. While later jurists debated whether this specific distance equates to two or four farsakhs (approx. 2-3 miles), the narration emphasizes the importance of observable natural phenomena in establishing religious obligations. It reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of linking fiqh rulings to the lived reality and topography of the Prophet's time.
